title: Evaluating Elevated D-Dimer Levels Associated Clinical Conditions in Hospitalised Patients: A Cross-sectional Study
abstract: Introduction: D-dimer is widely used to exclude Venous Thromboembolism (VTE) and to support the diagnosis of Disseminated Intravascular Coagulation (DIC). However, Elevated plasma D-dimer levels are not specific to thromboembolic disorders and may be observed in several non-thrombotic conditions such as infections, malignancies, inflammatory disorders, trauma, and postoperative states. This broad range of associated conditions complicates the interpretation of D-dimer results, particularly in resource-limited rural settings where the burden of infectious and inflammatory diseases is relatively high. Aim: To study the clinical conditions associated with elevated plasma D-dimer levels in hospitalised patients. Materials and Methods: The present cross-sectional, retrospective, laboratory database-based study was conducted in the Department of Pathology at a rural tertiary-care medical college in Western Maharashtra, India, from 1st October 2023 to 30th September 2024. Patients were selected from the Laboratory Information System (LIS) database based on records of quantitative plasma D-dimer testing performed during the study period. All consecutive hospitalised patients with at least one D-dimer value greater than 250 μg/L D-dimer Units (DDU), which represents the upper reference limit in the study laboratory, were included in the study. Demographic details, final clinical diagnosis, and selected laboratory parameters including Haemoglobin (Hb), Total Leukocyte Count (TLC), platelet count, Prothrombin Time/International Normalised Ratio (PT/INR), Activated Partial Thromboplastin Time (APTT), C-Reactive Protein (CRP), and other available laboratory investigations were retrieved from hospital records. Data were analysed using descriptive statistics. Results: Among 349 D-dimer tests, 247 were >250 μg/L DDU. After excluding duplicate tests (n=6) and cases with insufficient clinical information (n=6), 235 patients were analysed (139 males, 59.1%; 96 females, 40.9%). D-dimer values ranged from 255 to 75,860 μg/L DDU (mean 2,604.3 μg/L). The commonest cause was dengue (133/235, 56.6%), comprising 129 NS1 antigen-positive and 4 IgM-positive cases. Cardiovascular disorders {Myocardial infarction, Atrial Fibrillation, post Coronary artery bypass graft surgery (CABG)} constituted 28/235 (11.9%), followed by sepsis (16/235, 6.8%) and thromboembolic conditions (12/235, 5.1%). Other causes included Acute Respiratory Distress Syndrome (ARDS), fracture/osteomyelitis, pregnancy-related conditions, malignancy, snakebite and acute febrile illness. Overall mortality was 35/235 (14.9%) and was predominantly seen in patients with moderate-to-severe D-dimer elevation. Conclusion: In the current rural hospital cohort, elevated D-dimer levels were most frequently associated with infectious conditions particularly dengue followed by cardiovascular disorders and sepsis, whereas confirmed thromboembolic events represented a small proportion of cases. Extremely high values were observed in severe systemic illnesses such as sepsis and snakebite and were associated with poorer outcomes. These findings suggest that, in tropical rural settings, elevated D-dimer often reflects infection-related coagulation activation rather than isolated thromboembolism. Clinical interpretation should therefore be guided by the underlying disease context.

title: Downregulation of thioredoxin-like 1 contributes to miconazole’s antiviral activity against West Nile virus
abstract: Introduction West Nile virus (WNV)-associated neurological diseases pose a global public health burden, yet no approved antiviral treatments are available. This is primarily due to the challenges of crossing the blood-brain barrier and the lengthy, costly process of drug development. Methods High-throughput screening of a blood-brain barrier-penetrating FDA-approved compound library was performed to identify anti-WNV candidates in a neuronal cell infection model. Antiviral efficacy was further evaluated across different target cells and a range of flaviviruses, as well as in a mouse model of central nervous system (CNS) WNV infection. Stage-of-action analysis and mechanistic studies were conducted. Results Miconazole emerged as a promising candidate with significant antiviral efficacy against multiple flaviviruses in different cell types. In the CNS infection mouse model, miconazole treatment reduced viral load in brain tissue and improved survival rates. The compound primarily inhibited viral replication, without affecting binding, internalization, or membrane fusion. Mechanistic studies suggested that this antiviral effect may be mediated through the downregulation of host protein thioredoxin-like 1 (TXNL1). Discussion Our findings highlight miconazole as a promising candidate for repurposing in anti-flavivirus therapy and identify TXNL1 as a potential host target for the development of broad-spectrum antivirals.

Discussion Our findings highlight miconazole as a promising candidate for repurposing in anti-flavivirus therapy and identify TXNL1 as a potential host target for the development of broad-spectrum antivirals.

title: Incorporating vertical transmission into mechanistic modeling of West Nile virus for optimized control in Germany
abstract: West Nile virus is an arbovirus transmitted by infected Culex mosquitoes to birds, horses, and humans. Since its first recorded case in Germany in 2018, WNV has been endemic in several parts of Germany. Globalization, ecosystem modification and climate change have been identified as significant drivers of the arbovirus spread. However, vertical transmission of pathogens from adult female to their progeny might alter the transmission dynamics. In this study, we designed a process-based epidemic model incorporating climatic variables and epidemiological parameters that replicated mosquito populations and pathogen transmission between mosquito vectors and hosts, explicitly accounting for the role of vertical transmission. In addition, we evaluated the efficiency of biological, chemical, and mechanical strategies for mosquito population control. Our findings revealed that while vertical transmission marginally influenced West Nile virus transmission, the impact was more pronounced in endemic regions, signaling a relationship between vertical transmission and West Nile virus persistence. Among control methods implemented, the biological control method performed optimally and emerged as the preferred method over mechanical and chemical methods, respectively. This model provides an understanding on the impact of vertical transmission in mosquito-borne disease epidemiology and provides insights into the efficiency of mosquito control strategies which would support optimized implementation of mosquito management programs.

title: Peptidthioester und Peptidtriazolderivate durch Duale Modifikation von Peptidthiosulfonaten auf dem Harz
abstract: ZUSAMMENFASSUNG Modifizierte Peptide stellen aufgrund ihrer hohen Spezifität und Affinität insbesondere gegenüber pharmakologischen Zielstrukturen, die mit herkömmlichen kleinen Molekülen nicht behandelbar sind, eine wichtige Wirkstoffklasse dar. Daher sind Methoden, die eine effiziente Diversifizierung von Peptiden mit nicht‐kanonischen Modifikationen ermöglichen, sehr gefragt. Eine mögliche Strategie zur Erzeugung diversifizierter Peptide ist die Modifikation im späten Synthesestadium auf dem Harz, bei der eine funktionelle Gruppe – typischerweise in einer Aminosäureseitenkette oder am N‐Terminus – gezielt nach dem Aufbau der Peptidkette modifiziert wird, während die anderen funktionellen Gruppen geschützt bleiben. Hier stellen wir einen Ansatz zur dualen Modifikation im späten Synthesestadium auf dem Harz vor. Dieser Ansatz umfasst eine Reaktionssequenz aus kupferkatalysierter S‐Alkinylierung eines harzgebundenen Peptidthiosulfonats, gefolgt von einer iridiumkatalysierten Azid‐Alkin‐Click‐Reaktion (IrAAC). Auf diese Weise werden Peptide mit komplexen nicht‐kanonischen Modifikationen generiert. Der Ansatz der dualen Modifikation ist hochgradig modular und mit einer breiten Palette von Alkinen für die S‐Alkinylierung sowie von Aziden für die IrAAC kompatibel. Darüber hinaus kann diese Chemie zur Modifikation komplexer Peptide, wie beispielsweise der 34 Aminosäuren umfassenden WW‐Domäne, genutzt werden. In einer Struktur‐Wirkungs‐Beziehungsstudie zu triazolhaltigen Peptid‐Protease‐Inhibitoren des Dengue‐Virus demonstrieren wir das große Potenzial der modularen dualen Modifikation von Peptidthiosulfonaten auf dem Harz zur Modulation von Peptid‐Protein‐Wechselwirkungen.

analysis.research_question_and_background: The study addresses the need for efficient diversification of peptides with non-canonical modifications to target pharmacological structures that are not treatable with conventional small molecules.
analysis.study_design_and_population: The research presents a novel approach for dual modification of peptides on resin, demonstrated through a structure-activity relationship study with triazole-containing peptide-protease inhibitors targeting the Dengue virus.
analysis.methods: The method involves a reaction sequence of copper-catalyzed S-alkynylation of a resin-bound peptidthiosulfonate, followed by an iridium-catalyzed azide-alkyne click reaction (IrAAC), enabling the generation of peptides with complex non-canonical modifications.
analysis.main_results: The approach successfully generates peptides with complex non-canonical modifications and is highly modular, compatible with a wide range of alkynes and azides, and applicable to complex peptides such as the 34-amino acid WW-domain.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The authors interpret the dual modification strategy as having great potential for modulating peptide-protein interactions, as demonstrated in a study with triazole-containing peptide-protease inhibitors of the Dengue virus.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings inform the development of novel peptide-based therapeutics for Dengue virus, potentially enabling the design of more effective inhibitors targeting viral proteases.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The evidence strength is moderate, as the study is limited to in vitro demonstrations and does not include in vivo validation or clinical data.

analysis.summary_en: This study introduces a novel dual modification approach for peptides on resin, utilizing copper-catalyzed S-alkynylation and iridium-catalyzed azide-alkyne click reactions to generate peptides with complex non-canonical modifications. The method is highly modular and compatible with various alkynes and azides, as demonstrated with a 34-amino acid WW-domain and a structure-activity relationship study of triazole-containing peptide-protease inhibitors targeting the Dengue virus. The findings highlight the potential of this strategy for modulating peptide-protein interactions, offering a promising avenue for developing novel therapeutics against Dengue virus, though further in vivo validation is needed.

elements_zh.study_design_and_population: 该研究提出了一种在树脂上对肽进行双重修饰的新方法,通过针对 登革病毒 的含三唑肽蛋白酶抑制剂的结构-活性关系研究证明了这一方法。

elements_zh.interpretation_and_novelty: 作者将双重修饰策略解释为在调节肽-蛋白质相互作用方面具有巨大潜力,正如对 登革病毒 的含三唑肽-蛋白酶抑制剂的研究所证明的那样。
elements_zh.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: 这些发现为 登革病毒 新型肽疗法的开发提供了信息,有可能使设计更有效的针对病毒蛋白酶的抑制剂成为可能。
elements_zh.limitations_and_evidence_strength: 证据强度中等,因为该研究仅限于体外演示,不包括体内验证或临床数据。

abstract_zh: 摘要 改性肽由于其高特异性和亲和力,特别是对于常规小分子无法治疗的药理学靶标,构成了一类重要的活性成分。因此,能够实现肽与非典型修饰高效多样化的方法非常受欢迎。生成多样化肽的一种可能策略是在树脂上的合成后期进行修饰,即在构建肽链后,有选择性地修饰一个官能团——通常在氨基酸侧链或N端——而其他官能团保持受保护状态。在此,我们提出了一种在树脂上进行双重合成后期修饰的方法。该方法包括一个反应序列,首先对树脂结合的肽硫代磺酸酯进行铜催化S-炔基化,随后进行铱催化叠氮-炔点击反应(IrAAC)。通过这种方式,生成了具有复杂非典型修饰的肽。这种双重修饰方法具有高度模块化,并与用于S-炔基化的多种炔烃以及用于IrAAC的多种叠氮化物兼容。此外,这种化学方法可用于修饰复杂的肽,例如由34个氨基酸组成的WW结构域。在针对登革病毒含三唑肽蛋白酶抑制剂的结构-活性关系研究中,我们展示了树脂上肽硫代磺酸酯的模块化双重修饰在调节肽-蛋白相互作用方面的巨大潜力。

analysis_zh.main_results: 该方法成功生成了具有复杂非规范修饰的肽,并且高度模块化,与多种炔烃和叠氮化物兼容,并且适用于复杂肽,例如 34 个氨基酸的 WW 结构域。
analysis_zh.interpretation_and_novelty: 作者将双重修饰策略解释为在调节肽-蛋白质相互作用方面具有巨大潜力,正如对 登革病毒 的含三唑肽-蛋白酶抑制剂的研究所证明的那样。
analysis_zh.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: 这些发现为 登革病毒 新型肽疗法的开发提供了信息,有可能使设计更有效的针对病毒蛋白酶的抑制剂成为可能。
analysis_zh.limitations_and_evidence_strength: 证据强度中等,因为该研究仅限于体外演示,不包括体内验证或临床数据。

Volume 32, Number 8—August 2026 Dispatch Detection of Dengue Virus in Aedes aegypti Mosquitoes, Dubai, United Arab Emirates Suggested citation for this article Abstract We performed a 1-year mosquito survey in Dubai, United Arab Emirates, after a dengue virus outbreak in 2024. We collected 1,598 Aedes aegypti mosquitoes and detected dengue virus in 5 pools of <20 mosquitoes. Our findings underscore the importance of sustained vector surveillance for dengue virus in arid urban environments. During the past few decades, mosquitoborne diseases have increased worldwide, partly because of the spread of competent mosquito vectors. Changes in climate are among the primary factors contributing to the expanded ranges of arbovirus vector mosquitoes into temperate zones (1). Meanwhile, arid regions with extremely hot summers, such as the Gulf countries of the Arabian Peninsula, were not colonized by invasive mosquitoes until recently, likely because of increased urbanization (2). Dengue fever is a mosquitoborne disease caused by dengue virus (DENV) and monitored through regional and international surveillance systems. Increased dengue activity, including autochthonous cases, was reported in the United Arab Emirates (UAE) after periods of increased rainfall in April 2024 (3). To monitor local mosquito species and identify circulating mosquitoborne viruses, we conducted a mosquito survey in Dubai, UAE. To investigate the spread and distribution pattern of Aedes aegypti mosquitoes in the city of Dubai, we initiated a targeted mosquito survey. We evaluated the trapped mosquitoes for the presence of mosquitoborne human pathogens by using molecular techniques. Mosquito trapping was part of an enhanced Dubai Municipality Public Health Services Department mosquito surveillance program. We started the entomologic survey on June 20, 2024, and continued it for 1 year. Our trapping method was opportunistic, designed to sample Ae. aegypti mosquitoes in urban areas, specifically targeting labor camps, construction sites, residential communities, and green spaces including parks, stables, ponds and lakes, and gardens. We placed BG-Sentinel mosquito traps (Biogents, https://us-shop.biogents.com) without a light source throughout the city of Dubai combined with CO2 lures. We conducted trapping over 3 days at 60 sites, each sampled 1–33 times (mean 4.3 times, median 2 times), with 1–7 sites (mean 1.9 sites, median 1 site)sampled per trapping period. We collected and transferred the trap contents to the Public Health Pest Control Section laboratory of Dubai Municipality. We identified Ae. aegypti and Anopheles stephensi mosquitoes morphologically (4; World Health Organization, https://iris.who.int/handle/10665/334210) and identified other mosquitoes to genus level. We pooled <20 mosquitoes per vial and froze the vials at –50°C. We homogenized mosquito pools in 500 μL of phosphate buffered saline with stainless steel beads (Benchmark Scientific, https://www.benchmarkscientific.com) on a Bead Mill homogenizer (OMNI International, https://www.fishersci.com). We extracted viral nucleic acid from mosquitoes by using a Quick-RNA Viral Kit (Zymo Research, https://www.zymoresearch.com) according to manufacturer instructions. We screened Ae. aegypti mosquitoes for dengue, chikungunya, Zika, yellow fever, Rift Valley fever, and Alkhurma hemorrhagic fever virus nucleic acids by using virus-specific quantitative reverse transcription PCR (qRT-PCR) kits (altona Diagnostics, https://altona-diagnostics.com). We retested and serotyped all samples positive for DENV by using the RealStar Dengue Type qRT-PCR Kit 1.0 (altona Diagnostics). We screened Culex spp., Aedes, and Ochlerotatus spp. mosquitoes for West Nile, Rift valley fever, and Alkhurma hemorragic fever virus nucleic acids by using the corresponding RealStar qRT-PCR Kits (altona Diagnostics). We also screened An. stephensi mosquitoes for Plasmodia parasites by using the RealStar Malaria Screen & Type PCR kit 1.0 (altona Diagnostics). We used a bias-corrected maximum likelihood estimate of minimum infection rate on the basis of variable size pooling with the package binGroup v2.2-1 in R version 4.3.3 (The R Project for Statistical Computing, https://www.r-project.org). We collected a total of 3,743 adult mosquitoes over 263 trapping periods: 1,598 Ae. aegypti, 1,555 Culex spp., 376 Ochlerotatus spp., and 214 An. stephensi. We found Ae. aegypti mosquitoes throughout Dubai, mainly collected from labor camps, construction sites, and green spaces. Compared with other mosquito species sampled, we found fewer An. stephensi mosquitoes in periurban areas with aquatic habitats (Figure 1). We observed seasonal variability in the number of mosquitoes collected, with the lowest number collected during the summer months (Figure 2). We detected DENV in 5 of 151 Ae. aegypti pools: 3 pools with DENV-1 and 2 with DENV-2. The field minimum infection rate was 3.1 (95% CI 0.4–5.9)/1,000 mosquitoes . We detected DENV-2 in the last week of June (epidemiologic week 26 of 2024) near the main Dubai airport (Figure 2). We detected both DENV-1 and DENV-2 from mid-November through mid-December (epidemiologic weeks 47–50 of 2024) in the southwest Al Hebiah 5 district (Figure 2). We did not detect any other viruses in the other mosquito pools, and we did not find Plasmodia parasites in any of the mosquito pools with An. stephensi mosquitoes. In most of the Gulf countries, the workforce is recruited from countries in which dengue, chikungunya, Zika, yellow fever, Rift Valley fever or West Nile virus are endemic, and imported cases were previously reported in the Arabian Peninsula. Dengue fever outbreaks in the Arabian Peninsula have occurred in Yemen and the Jeddah and Mecca region of Saudi Arabia (5). Oman, which borders UAE, experienced its first autochthonous dengue outbreak during December 2018 through mid-March 2019, with 59 reported cases (6). A second autochthonous outbreak occurred from mid-March through mid-April 2022 and involved 169 locally acquired cases (7). In the UAE, neither Aedes (Stegomyia) mosquitoes nor locally acquired dengue cases were reported in recent decades (5). Historically, there was evidence of Ae. aegypti mosquitoes in UAE as early as 1944 (8). However, it is assumed that the populations of Ae. aegypti mosquitoes from older records would not have survived the liberal use of insecticides in the second half of the 1900s (9). We did not find Ae. aegypti mosquitoes in our entomologic survey conducted during January–May 2018 in the UAE (10). The first recent record of an Ae. aegypti mosquito in Dubai was in May 2016, identified by the Public Health Pest Control Section laboratory, Dubai Municipality, and confirmed by the British Natural History Museum. Other Gulf countries such as Qatar also reported recent, yet sporadic, evidence of Ae. aegypti mosquitoes (11). Regional and global species distribution models have indicated that urban areas in Gulf countries are suitable for Ae. aegypti mosquitoes (12). Likely, the increased DENV activity we observed was driven by a recently established Ae. aegypti population in Dubai. In recent years, increased frequency of heavy rainfall with flooding and stagnant surface water were recorded worldwide including the Gulf countries, contributing to an increase in mosquito abundance and dengue cases (13). In addition, manmade water-containing vessels can serve as reservoirs for immature Ae. aegypti mosquitoes and correlate with cases of dengue fever (14). Those sources of water in arid environments likely contribute to extended mosquito survival during dry periods (15). Our results demonstrate the widespread distribution of Ae. aegypti mosquitoes in Dubai. We detected DENV-1 and DENV-2 in Ae. aegypti mosquitoes from 2 sampling locations within the urban area of Dubai, which coincided with a DENV-2 outbreak in humans (Dubai Health, unpub. data). Our findings demonstrate the value of integrated entomologic and molecular surveillance for early detection of mosquitoborne pathogens in arid urban settings. Future studies should establish seasonality and habitat associations to assist with mosquito control. The presence of Ae. aegypti mosquitos in urban areas in the Gulf region necessitates steps to reduce or eliminate DENV transmission. Efforts should include educating the public on avoiding mosquitoes, surveillance and targeted mosquito control, and isolating infected individuals quickly to prevent spread. Dr. Nowotny is professor of virology at the University of Veterinary Medicine, Vienna, Austria, and visiting professor at the College of Medicine, Mohammed Bin Rashid University of Medicine and Health Sciences, Dubai Health, Dubai, UAE. His research interests include emerging, zoonotic, and mosquitoborne virus infections. analysis.research_question_and_background: Increased dengue activity, including autochthonous cases, was reported in the United Arab Emirates after periods of increased rainfall in April 2024. To monitor local mosquito species and identify circulating mosquitoborne viruses, we conducted a mosquito survey in Dubai, UAE.
analysis.study_design_and_population: We performed a 1-year mosquito survey in Dubai, United Arab Emirates, starting on June 20, 2024. We collected 1,598 Aedes aegypti mosquitoes using opportunistic trapping with BG-Sentinel mosquito traps combined with CO2 lures. The survey targeted urban areas including labor camps, construction sites, residential communities, and green spaces.
analysis.methods: We evaluated the trapped mosquitoes for the presence of mosquitoborne human pathogens by using molecular techniques. Mosquito trapping was part of an enhanced Dubai Municipality Public Health Services Department mosquito surveillance program. We detected dengue virus in 5 pools of < 20 mosquitoes.
analysis.main_results: We collected 1,598 Aedes aegypti mosquitoes and detected dengue virus in 5 pools of < 20 mosquitoes. The supplied evidence does not report specific infection rates, serotype distributions, or statistical comparisons.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: Our findings underscore the importance of sustained vector surveillance for dengue virus in arid urban environments. The detection of dengue virus in Aedes aegypti mosquitoes confirms local transmission potential following the 2024 outbreak.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: These results highlight the need for ongoing vector surveillance to manage dengue virus risks in arid urban settings like Dubai. Public health efforts should focus on monitoring mosquito populations in labor camps, construction sites, and green spaces to prevent future outbreaks.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The supplied evidence does not report specific study limitations or a detailed assessment of evidence strength. The opportunistic trapping method may limit the generalizability of the findings to all urban areas in Dubai.

analysis.summary_en: Following a dengue outbreak in 2024, this study conducted a one-year entomologic survey in Dubai, UAE, to monitor local mosquito species and circulating viruses. Using BG-Sentinel traps with CO2 lures, researchers collected 1,598 Aedes aegypti mosquitoes from urban areas, including labor camps and green spaces. Molecular evaluation detected dengue virus in 5 pools of fewer than 20 mosquitoes. These findings underscore the importance of sustained vector surveillance in arid urban environments to identify and mitigate local transmission risks. The study highlights the need for targeted public health monitoring in specific urban settings to manage dengue activity effectively.

analysis_en.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: These results highlight the need for ongoing vector surveillance to manage dengue virus risks in arid urban settings like Dubai. Public health efforts should focus on monitoring mosquito populations in labor camps, construction sites, and green spaces to prevent future outbreaks.
analysis_en.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The supplied evidence does not report specific study limitations or a detailed assessment of evidence strength. The opportunistic trapping method may limit the generalizability of the findings to all urban areas in Dubai.

full_text: Les moustiques invasifs ne constituent pas seulement une menace sanitaire : ils représentent aussi un coût économique majeur. Une étude internationale estime qu’entre 1975 et 2020, les maladies transmises par les moustiques Aedes ont engendré au moins 94,7 milliards de dollars de pertes dans le monde. Plus frappant encore, les dépenses consacrées à la prévention restent très inférieures aux coûts supportés une fois les épidémies déclarées. Ils sont petits, à peine visibles, et pourtant leur impact économique atteint une ampleur comparable à celle de certaines crises sanitaires majeures. Les moustiques invasifs du genre Aedes – notamment Aedes albopictus (moustique tigre) et Aedes aegypti (son cousin, moins connu en Europe, le moustique de la fièvre jaune)- ne se contentent pas de troubler nos soirées estivales, ils nous transmettent les virus de la dengue, de la fièvre jaune, chikungunya ou encore Zika et, ce faisant, ils engendrent également des coûts considérables pour les systèmes de santé, les collectivités et les ménages du monde entier. Dans une étude publiée en 2024 dans Science of The Total Environment on estime qu’entre 1975 et 2020, les coûts économiques liés à ces moustiques et aux maladies qu’ils transmettent, atteignent au minimum 94,7 milliards (en dollars de 2022). Les estimations hautes suggèrent elles un coût total supérieur à 300 milliards lorsque les séquelles à long terme sont prises en compte, soit un montant comparable au coût total de l’ouragan Katrina, l’une des catastrophes naturelles les plus coûteuses de l’histoire contemporaine, et supérieur à ceux de la catastrophe pétrolière de Deepwater Horizon en 2010 dans le golfe du Mexique. Derrière ce chiffre impressionnant, on trouve une réalité plus préoccupante encore : cette évaluation est sans doute largement sous-estimée et, contrairement à une catastrophe ponctuelle, ces coûts s’accumulent année après année. Et surtout, elle révèle un déséquilibre majeur dans nos choix collectifs : nous dépensons beaucoup plus pour réparer les dégâts que pour prévenir les crises, environ dix fois plus. Une expansion silencieuse, un coût croissant Pour comprendre ces montants colossaux, il faut d’abord regarder l’expansion silencieuse des moustiques concernés. Issus de régions tropicales, les moustiques Aedes ont étendu leur aire de répartition à un rythme soutenu. Aedes aegypti, originaire d’Afrique, est aujourd’hui présent dans une grande partie des régions tropicales et subtropicales d’Amérique, d’Asie et d’Océanie. Son aire de répartition s’est progressivement étendue sous l’effet des échanges commerciaux et de l’urbanisation. Aedes albopictus, le moustique tigre, lui, a colonisé le monde plus tardivement, à partir des années 1970, en provenance d’Asie. Portés par la mondialisation des échanges (commerce international, transport maritime et aérien), l’urbanisation rapide et souvent mal planifiée, ainsi que par le réchauffement climatique, ces vecteurs de virus se sont implantés sur tous les continents, y compris en Europe et en Amérique du Nord. Leur succès écologique a une conséquence directe : l’augmentation du nombre d’épidémies. La dengue, autrefois confinée à certaines régions tropicales, est devenue l’une des maladies virales à transmission vectorielle les plus répandues au monde. Présente dans plus de 100 pays, elle connaît des flambées de plus en plus fréquentes et de plus en plus importantes, avec des niveaux records observés ces dernières années. En 2023 et 2024, plusieurs pays d’Amérique latine, dont le Brésil et l’Argentine, ont enregistré des épidémies historiques comptant plusieurs millions de cas. Le chikungunya et le Zika ont provoqué des crises sanitaires majeures depuis le début des années 2000, avec des répercussions sanitaires durables, notamment des complications neurologiques et congénitales. Cette crise sanitaire est aussi une crise économique, dont les conséquences restent largement sous-estimées dans le débat public. 94,7 milliards de dollars : une estimation minimale Notre équipe a compilé les données issues de la base internationale InvaCost) qui recense les coûts économiques associés aux espèces invasives. Sur une période de 45 ans (1975-2020), nous avons identifié au moins 94,7 milliards de dollars (soit environ 105 milliards en dollars 2026) de coûts cumulés liés aux moustiques Aedes et aux maladies qu’ils transmettent. Cela représente en moyenne plus de 3 milliards de dollars par an, avec des pics spectaculaires : en 2013, la facture a dépassé les 20 milliards de dollars. Ces montants incluent plusieurs types de dépenses : les coûts médicaux (hospitalisations, consultations, traitements), les pertes de productivité liées aux arrêts de travail, les dépenses publiques de surveillance et de lutte antivectorielle (limitation des populations de moustiques par divers moyens dont les campagnes de participation communautaire pour la réduction d’eaux stagnantes, les larvicides, où les insecticides), ainsi que certains impacts économiques indirects (comme l’absentéisme ou des baisses de productivité). La dengue représente à elle seule près de 80 % des coûts totaux estimés. Le chikungunya et le Zika, bien que plus ponctuels dans leur émergence, contribuent également de manière significative dans la dernière décennie, reflétant plusieurs grandes crises épidémiques sur la période. Mais ces chiffres impressionnants ne représentent pourtant qu’une partie de la réalité. Une sous-estimation structurelle De fait, les 94,7 milliards de dollars identifiés ne représentent que les coûts documentés et publiés dans la littérature scientifique ou institutionnelle. Il ne s’agit pas d’estimations ni d’extrapolations. Or, de nombreux pays, notamment à revenu faible ou intermédiaire, ne disposent pas des moyens pour mesurer et documenter ces impacts économiques. Les dépenses informelles des ménages, les pertes économiques non déclarées, les conséquences à long terme sur la santé (handicaps, troubles neurologiques, complications congénitales liées au Zika), ou encore les effets sur le tourisme et l’attractivité économique (le nombre de visiteurs chute drastiquement dans les pays connaissant une épidémie) sont rarement quantifiés. Autrement dit, la facture réelle pourrait être bien plus élevée. Ce biais révèle en outre une inégalité structurelle : les pays les plus touchés sont souvent ceux qui disposent des systèmes de surveillance les moins robustes, en particulier dans plusieurs régions d’Asie du Sud-Est, d’Afrique subsaharienne et d’Amérique latine. Le manque de données n’est pas synonyme d’absence de coût : il traduit plutôt une invisibilisation économique des régions les plus vulnérables. Réagir et soigner plutôt que prévenir : un choix coûteux Anticiper ces conséquences et investir dans la prévention, la surveillance et la gestion intégrée des vecteurs apparaît donc essentiel pour limiter les effets sanitaires, économiques et sociaux des futures épidémies. Les données montrent cependant que les coûts liés aux « dommages et pertes » – c’est-à-dire les conséquences des maladies une fois qu’elles surviennent – sont largement supérieurs aux dépenses consacrées à la prévention et à la gestion. En d’autres termes, on dépense beaucoup plus en réaction aux épidémies que pour les empêcher. Les campagnes de démoustication, la surveillance entomologique, l’amélioration des infrastructures urbaines (gestion des eaux stagnantes, assainissement), ou encore la recherche sur les méthodes innovantes de contrôle des populations de moustiques (comme la dissémination de moustiques porteurs de Wolbachia ou de mâles stériles) restent sous-financées par rapport à l’ampleur des dommages constatés. Ce déséquilibre pose une question centrale de politique publique : pourquoi attendons-nous que la crise éclate pour agir ? Read more: Les lâchers de moustiques modifiés pour lutter contre la dengue, le chikungunya ou la fièvre jaune La réponse est en partie politique et budgétaire. Les dépenses de prévention sont souvent moins visibles, moins médiatisées, et leurs bénéfices sont difficiles à attribuer directement. À l’inverse, les coûts des épidémies apparaissent brutalement dans les statistiques hospitalières et économiques. Mais cette logique court-termiste se révèle économiquement inefficace. Les données montrent pourtant qu’un investissement accru dans la prévention pourrait réduire significativement la charge économique globale à long terme. Une problématique sociale mondiale Au-delà des chiffres, l’enjeu est profondément social. Les maladies transmises par les moustiques Aedes touchent de manière disproportionnée les populations urbaines défavorisées, vivant dans des environnements où l’accès à l’eau potable, à l’assainissement et aux infrastructures sanitaires est limité. Les inégalités socio-économiques favorisent la prolifération des moustiques : stockage d’eau dans des récipients ouverts, absence de systèmes d’évacuation performants, habitat dense et précaire. Les populations les plus vulnérables cumulent donc les risques sanitaires et les pertes économiques. Lorsqu’un membre d’un foyer tombe malade, les conséquences dépassent le simple coût médical : perte de revenus, déscolarisation temporaire des enfants, endettement pour financer les soins. À l’échelle collective, ces micro-chocs économiques s’additionnent pour former un fardeau macroéconomique. La mondialisation du phénomène ajoute une dimension supplémentaire : même les pays tempérés, longtemps considérés comme à l’abri, voient désormais l’implantation durable de Aedes albopictus. Les épisodes autochtones de dengue ou de chikungunya en Europe illustrent cette nouvelle réalité et les récentes projections climatiques suggèrent que le potentiel de transmission pourrait encore s’étendre dans les décennies à venir. La question n’est plus celle d’un « problème tropical », mais d’un enjeu global. Read more: Virus « exotiques » dans l’Hexagone : Que faut-il savoir du chikungunya ? Une alerte et une opportunité Cette lecture économique permet de renouveler notre compréhension d’un problème souvent abordé sous le seul angle sanitaire. En mettant un coût sur les conséquences des invasions de moustiques Aedes, cette étude déplace le débat vers le terrain des politiques publiques et des arbitrages budgétaires. Les moustiques ne sont pas seulement une nuisance estivale. Ils représentent un coût structurel croissant pour les systèmes de santé, les économies nationales et les ménages. Dans un monde marqué par l’intensification des échanges et les bouleversements climatiques, ils illustrent une réalité concrète : certains impacts économiques des transformations environnementales ne sont ni abstraits ni lointains. Ils se traduisent en milliards de dollars, en inégalités sociales accrues et en systèmes de santé sous tension. Reconnaître l’ampleur économique du phénomène conduit ainsi à changer de perspective : dans un contexte de mondialisation des échanges et de changement climatique, la lutte antivectorielle n’est plus seulement une mesure de santé publique. Elle constitue un investissement collectif destiné à éviter des coûts sanitaires, sociaux et économiques bien plus élevés demain.

Sur une période de 45 ans (1975-2020), nous avons identifié au moins 94,7 milliards de dollars (soit environ 105 milliards en dollars 2026) de coûts cumulés liés aux moustiques Aedes et aux maladies qu’ils transmettent. Cela représente en moyenne plus de 3 milliards de dollars par an, avec des pics spectaculaires : en 2013, la facture a dépassé les 20 milliards de dollars. Ces montants incluent plusieurs types de dépenses : les coûts médicaux (hospitalisations, consultations, traitements), les pertes de productivité liées aux arrêts de travail, les dépenses publiques de surveillance et de lutte antivectorielle (limitation des populations de moustiques par divers moyens dont les campagnes de participation communautaire pour la réduction d’eaux stagnantes, les larvicides, où les insecticides), ainsi que certains impacts économiques indirects (comme l’absentéisme ou des baisses de productivité). La dengue représente à elle seule près de 80 % des coûts totaux estimés. Le chikungunya et le Zika, bien que plus ponctuels dans leur émergence, contribuent également de manière significative dans la dernière décennie, reflétant plusieurs grandes crises épidémiques sur la période. Mais ces chiffres impressionnants ne représentent pourtant qu’une partie de la réalité. Une sous-estimation structurelle De fait, les 94,7 milliards de dollars identifiés ne représentent que les coûts documentés et publiés dans la littérature scientifique ou institutionnelle. Il ne s’agit pas d’estimations ni d’extrapolations. Or, de nombreux pays, notamment à revenu faible ou intermédiaire, ne disposent pas des moyens pour mesurer et documenter ces impacts économiques. Les dépenses informelles des ménages, les pertes économiques non déclarées, les conséquences à long terme sur la santé (handicaps, troubles neurologiques, complications congénitales liées au Zika), ou encore les effets sur le tourisme et l’attractivité économique (le nombre de visiteurs chute drastiquement dans les pays connaissant une épidémie) sont rarement quantifiés. Autrement dit, la facture réelle pourrait être bien plus élevée. Ce biais révèle en outre une inégalité structurelle : les pays les plus touchés sont souvent ceux qui disposent des systèmes de surveillance les moins robustes, en particulier dans plusieurs régions d’Asie du Sud-Est, d’Afrique subsaharienne et d’Amérique latine. Le manque de données n’est pas synonyme d’absence de coût : il traduit plutôt une invisibilisation économique des régions les plus vulnérables. Réagir et soigner plutôt que prévenir : un choix coûteux Anticiper ces conséquences et investir dans la prévention, la surveillance et la gestion intégrée des vecteurs apparaît donc essentiel pour limiter les effets sanitaires, économiques et sociaux des futures épidémies. Les données montrent cependant que les coûts liés aux « dommages et pertes » – c’est-à-dire les conséquences des maladies une fois qu’elles surviennent – sont largement supérieurs aux dépenses consacrées à la prévention et à la gestion. En d’autres termes, on dépense beaucoup plus en réaction aux épidémies que pour les empêcher. Les campagnes de démoustication, la surveillance entomologique, l’amélioration des infrastructures urbaines (gestion des eaux stagnantes, assainissement), ou encore la recherche sur les méthodes innovantes de contrôle des populations de moustiques (comme la dissémination de moustiques porteurs de Wolbachia ou de mâles stériles) restent sous-financées par rapport à l’ampleur des dommages constatés. Ce déséquilibre pose une question centrale de politique publique : pourquoi attendons-nous que la crise éclate pour agir ? analysis.research_question_and_background: Invasive Aedes mosquitoes pose a major public health threat and cause significant economic losses, yet prevention spending remains insufficient compared to outbreak response costs. This study aimed to quantify the global economic burden of Aedes-transmitted diseases, including dengue, and to highlight the disparity between reactive expenditures and preventive investments.
analysis.study_design_and_population: The authors compiled data from the international InvaCost database to assess economic costs associated with invasive species over a 45-year period from 1975 to 2020. The analysis focused on global costs related to Aedes mosquitoes and the diseases they transmit, including dengue, chikungunya, and Zika, across affected countries.
analysis.methods: The team identified and aggregated documented costs from scientific and institutional literature, converting figures to 2022 US dollars. The analysis included direct medical costs, lost productivity, public vector control expenditures, and indirect economic impacts, while noting that estimates likely represent a minimum due to underreporting.
analysis.main_results: The study estimated a minimum cumulative cost of 94.7 billion US dollars (approximately 105 billion in 2026 dollars) attributable to Aedes mosquitoes and their associated diseases between 1975 and 2020. Annual costs averaged over 3 billion dollars, with a peak exceeding 20 billion dollars in 2013, and high-end estimates including long-term sequelae suggested a total cost exceeding 300 billion dollars.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The authors interpreted these findings as evidence of a structural underestimation of economic impacts and a major imbalance in collective choices, noting that spending on damage repair is approximately ten times higher than on prevention. The cumulative, recurring nature of these costs distinguishes them from singular natural disasters like Hurricane Katrina.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: These findings underscore the critical need to shift resources from reaction to anticipation, emphasizing investments in integrated vector management, surveillance, urban infrastructure, and innovative control methods. Such preventive measures are essential to mitigate the future health, economic, and social consequences of Aedes-borne epidemics.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The evidence strength is moderate because the 94.7 billion dollar figure relies solely on documented and published costs, which likely represents a significant underestimation, particularly in regions with less robust surveillance systems like South-East Asia, Sub-Saharan Africa, and Latin America.

analysis.summary_en: This study quantified the global economic burden of invasive Aedes mosquitoes and the diseases they transmit, including dengue, by compiling data from the InvaCost database between 1975 and 2020. The researchers found a minimum cumulative cost of 94.7 billion US dollars, averaging over 3 billion dollars annually with a peak of 20 billion dollars in 2013, and noted that high-end estimates including long-term sequelae exceed 300 billion dollars. The analysis revealed a significant imbalance, as reactive spending is approximately ten times higher than investment in prevention. The authors conclude that these costs are structurally underestimated and advocate for increased funding for surveillance, urban infrastructure, and integrated vector management to mitigate future epidemics.

title: Spatial diffusion and climatic suitability shape West Nile Virus invasion risk across Europe
abstract: The expansion of West Nile virus (WNV), a mosquito-borne zoonotic flavivirus, across Europe is commonly attributed to eco-climatic drivers of transmission, yet these factors alone cannot explain why some disease-free regions become invaded while neighbouring, eco-climatically similar regions remain unaffected. Here we developed a spatial diffusion framework, integrated with time-to-event modelling, applied to fine-scale administrative regions in 18 European countries with reported WNV transmission between 2006 and 2024. We quantify how the nearest distance to existing invasion foci, cumulative neighbourhood invasion pressure, the intensity of WNV transmission in the nearest invaded region, and climatic suitability govern emergence of WNV in Europe. We show that 71% of first emergence events occurred within 150 km of an existing focus, with WNV invasion risk declining sharply at greater distance. In multivariable analyses, each 100 km of geographic isolation reduced the hazard of invasion by 44% on average (HR = 0.56, 95% CI 0.51–0.62), while cumulative neighbourhood invasion pressure independently increased it by 26% (HR = 1.26, 95% CI 1.16–1.35). Critically, warmer temperatures eroded the protective barrier of geographic distance, enabling WNV establishment in regions that would otherwise remain naïve. These findings define the spatial scale and climatic conditions governing pathogen invasion, offering a transferable framework for delineating invasion frontlines and strengthening early-warning systems for climate-sensitive vector-borne disease emergence.

Here we developed a spatial diffusion framework, integrated with time-to-event modelling, applied to fine-scale administrative regions in 18 European countries with reported WNV transmission between 2006 and 2024. We quantify how the nearest distance to existing invasion foci, cumulative neighbourhood invasion pressure, the intensity of WNV transmission in the nearest invaded region, and climatic suitability govern emergence of WNV in Europe. We show that 71% of first emergence events occurred within 150 km of an existing focus, with WNV invasion risk declining sharply at greater distance. In multivariable analyses, each 100 km of geographic isolation reduced the hazard of invasion by 44% on average (HR = 0.56, 95% CI 0.51–0.62), while cumulative neighbourhood invasion pressure independently increased it by 26% (HR = 1.26, 95% CI 1.16–1.35). These findings define the spatial scale and climatic conditions governing pathogen invasion, offering a transferable framework for delineating invasion frontlines and strengthening early-warning systems for climate-sensitive vector-borne disease emergence. Introduction The emergence of a zoonotic vector-borne disease in a previously naïve area is rarely a purely stochastic event. It requires the concurrent alignment of multiple circumstances: a prospect for pathogen introduction, a competent host, suitable and abundant vectors, climatic suitability and a local environment permissive enough for establishment and onward transmission1. Global environmental change accelerates the emergence and spread of vector-borne diseases and their eco-climatic drivers have been previously described1–3. Yet, the process of pathogen diffusion, from existing foci to naïve areas, has not been disentangled and quantified. This knowledge asymmetry between the eco-climatic permissiveness of disease transmission and spatial pathogen diffusion remains one of the most salient gaps in contemporary infectious disease ecology. This discrepancy is particularly apparent for West Nile virus (WNV) in Europe. Sporadic European WNV outbreaks were documented from the late twentieth century onward, including Bucharest, Romania (1996–1997), the Czech Republic (1997), and Volgograd, Russia (1999)4,5. Since its resurgence across Europe in the early twenty-first century, WNV has spread from a few endemic foci in southeastern Europe to invade much of the continent, with outbreaks now reported at higher latitudes and in areas with no prior history of local circulation 6–8. This expansion has transformed WNV from a local episodic pathogen into a continent-wide zoonotic threat, yet the underlying mechanisms governing its geographic spread into previously disease-free areas have not been formally quantified. Eco-climatic drivers of WNV circulation, including temperature, humidity, vector ecology, and avian host availability, are increasingly Page 2/26 well understood, and future projections of WNV risk under climate change have been described6,9–11. What these frameworks cannot explain is the frontline of WNV invasion: why a particular region transitions from a disease-free to invaded in a particular year, while eco-climatically similar neighbouring regions remain naive. Answering this question requires moving beyond environmental and climatic suitability alone to consider spatial diffusion, the process by which WNV propagates outward from established foci across geographic space. For WNV, the virus circulates in an enzootic cycle between Culex mosquitoes and birds, and its geographic spread reflects the cumulative influence of interconnected local and migratory avian host populations and their movements, short-range mosquito dispersal, and recurring introduction events from surrounding WNV invaded areas. The influence of an existing invasion foci on a naïve area is not binary, declining continuously with geographic distance rather than switching abruptly at administrative borders, and generates a spatially structured pattern of invaded and naïve areas that evolve as new areas become established12. Despite its importance, spatial diffusion has rarely been explicitly quantified in vector-borne disease epidemiology12. Most modelling frameworks treat geographic areas as independent units, characterise connectivity through administrative adjacency or binary neighbourhood relationships, or rely on phylogeographic reconstruction of viral lineage movement12–14. These approaches capture important aspects of pathogen spread but cannot directly quantify the epidemiological consequence of spatial diffusion: the probability that a naïve area transitions to an invaded state as a function of its position relative to existing invasion foci15. No framework currently exists that integrates an explicit, distance- decay spatial diffusion process with environmental suitability to model the trajectory of pathogen emergence at the regional scale. Here we develop such a framework and apply it to the 18-year expansion of WNV across Europe. We introduce three complementary spatial diffusion metrics, grounded in the ‘introduction effort’ (propagule pressure) of invasion ecology15: geographic proximity to the nearest previously invaded region12, which captures a region's position relative to the advancing invasion front; neighbourhood invasion pressure, a distance-decayed time-varying index of cumulative exposure to surrounding invaded regions that reflects the cumulative density of surrounding invasion; and source-region transmission intensity, which captures the magnitude of WNV transmission in the nearest invaded source region. Integrating these metrics with climatic suitability within a time-to-event survival modelling framework16, applied to 1,011 NUTS3 (Nomenclature of Territorial Units for Statistics, level 3) regions across 18 European countries from 2006 to 20248, we address three questions. First, are spatial diffusion metrics independent and dominant predictors of WNV invasion risk in naïve regions, over and above climatic suitability? Second, does invasion risk in a naïve region exhibit a characteristic spatial scale, a distance threshold, beyond which the diffusion-mediated risk becomes negligible? Third, does climatic suitability modify the spatial reach of diffusion, enabling successful WNV invasion at greater distances from existing foci under warmer conditions? Page 3/26 This framework can be extended beyond WNV. The core tension between connectivity and environmental permissiveness (between the opportunity for introduction and the conditions for establishment) is a general feature of pathogen invasion, relevant to any vector-borne disease expanding into new geographic territory. For WNV specifically, the primary vector (Culex pipiens) is already ubiquitous across much of Europe10, which means that the critical barrier for regional emergence is not vector establishment but virus introduction and local amplification16. This shifts the analytical focus squarely onto spatial diffusion as the proximate driver of invasion timing and geography. By quantifying this process explicitly: its spatial scale, its non-linear neighbourhood invasion pressure, and its interaction with climate, we provide a mechanistic foundation for anticipating where and when WNV will emerge next, and a transferable approach for delineating invasion trajectories of climate-driven vector- borne diseases under climate change. Results Spatiotemporal invasion of WNV across Europe Between 2006 and 2024, WNV expanded into previously disease-free regions across Europe, spreading from initial foci in southeastern Europe to invade much of the continent across much of the continent (Fig. 1). Early emergence was concentrated in Romania and Hungary, the principal invasion origins during 2006–2008, followed by rapid expansion across the Balkan Peninsula and Mediterranean basin. A major emergence wave occurred in Greece in 2010–2011, when 23 regions reported their first documented outbreaks within two transmission seasons5. Italy subsequently emerged as the largest secondary origin of spread, contributing the greatest cumulative number of newly invaded regions of any country in the dataset. From 2017 onwards, WNV expanded into previously unaffected regions across central, western, and southern Europe, including Germany, France, Spain, Turkey, and the Netherlands, marking the most extensive period of geographic range expansion in the study period, with 148 first invasions across 11 newly affected countries. By 2024, WNV had invaded 269 of the 1,011 regions under observation (26.6%) across 18 European countries based on confirmed locally acquired human infections; the actual number of regions with established WNV circulation may be higher, as enzootic transmission in avian or equid populations can precede or occur independently of human case detection. The spatiotemporal pattern is consistent with a combination of short-range local diffusion from established foci and episodic long- distance colonisation events that seeded new regional centres of WNV invasion foci. Spatial scale of WNV invasion risk: distance-decay and thresholds To characterise the spatial determinants of WNV invasion, we examined the distances at which the first outbreak occurred relative to the nearest previously invaded region (Fig. 2A). First invasion events were strongly concentrated at short distances from existing invasion foci: 121 of 269 first invasions (45%) Page 4/26 occurred within 75 km, 192 (71%) within 150 km, and 236 (88%) within 300 km. Only six invasions (2.2%) occurred beyond 500 km from any previously invaded region. This concentration of invasion events at short distances provides direct empirical evidence for a characteristic diffusion scale governing WNV expansion in Europe. Neighbourhood invasion pressure exhibited a pronounced exponential association with annual invasion probability (Fig. 2B). Regions in the lowest four deciles of invasion pressure experienced virtually no invasion events (annual invasion probability < 0.2%), while risk increased sharply in the upper deciles, reaching 6.5% per year in the highest decile. The contrast between the lowest and highest deciles, a greater than 100-fold difference in annual invasion probability, indicates that the accumulation of invaded regions in the surrounding area generates a threshold-like elevation of invasion risk that cannot be attributed to proximity to a source region alone. Spatial diffusion is the dominant predictor of WNV invasion risk Univariable Cox proportional hazards analyses confirmed that spatial diffusion metrics were the strongest predictors of first WNV emergence across all covariates examined (Table 1). Geographic distance to the nearest previously invaded region was inversely associated with invasion hazard: each additional 100 km of isolation reduced the hazard of first emergence by 51% (HR = 0.49, 95% CI 0.44– 0.54; p < 0.001). Neighbourhood invasion pressure showed the strongest positive association: each one standard-deviation increase was associated with an 55% higher invasion hazard (HR = 1.55, 95% CI 1.47–1.64; p < 0.001). Transmission intensity in the nearest invaded source region also showed a strong positive association (HR = 1.40, 95% CI 1.18–1.67; p < 0.001) with the invasion hazard. All the spatial diffusion metrics substantially outperformed all climatic and urbanization covariates in univariable analyses. Among climatic variables, higher annual mean temperature was associated with increased invasion risk (HR = 1.22 per °C, 95% CI 1.17–1.26; p < 0.001), while higher relative humidity was associated with modestly reduced risk (HR = 0.95 per %, 95% CI 0.93–0.96; p < 0.001). Precipitation showed a weaker but significant inverse association in univariable analysis (HR = 0.83, 95% CI 0.73–0.94; p = 0.004). Urbanization category was not significantly associated with invasion risk. Spline-based Cox regression revealed that the association between geographic distance and invasion hazard was markedly non-linear (Fig. 3B). Relative invasion hazard declined most steeply within the first 150 km from an existing focus, with the rate of decline flattening beyond this distance. Beyond 250–300 km, hazard remained consistently and substantially reduced, identifying 150–300 km as the characteristic spatial scale beyond which diffusion-mediated invasion risk becomes negligible. The Kaplan–Meier analysis by distance category corroborated this pattern (Fig. 3B, inset): regions within 75 km of an existing invasion focus experienced the most rapid and sustained loss of outbreak-free status across the study period, whereas regions located more than 500 km from any previously affected region Page 5/26 remained largely WNV-free throughout 2006–2024, underscoring the strong spatial constraints governing WNV regional spread. Geographic distance retained a pronounced negative association: each additional 100 km of distance from the nearest invaded region reduced the hazard of first emergence by 44% on average across the study period (HR = 0.56, 95% CI 0.50–0.62; p < 0.001). Neighbourhood invasion pressure independently increased emergence hazard by 26% on average across the study period, per standard-deviation increase (HR = 1.26, 95% CI 1.17–1.35; p < 0.001). Attenuation of the invasion pressure effect relative to univariable analyses, from HR 1.55 to 1.26, reflects partial confounding by temperature, consistent with the expectation that warmer regions tend to be geographically proximate to established endemic foci. The inclusion of WNV transmission intensity in the nearest invaded source region provided additional predictive information beyond geographic proximity and cumulative pressure. Not only did it significantly improve model fit (ΔAIC = 12.2; likelihood-ratio p < 0.001), but it also independently elevated invasion Page 6/26 hazard after full adjustment (HR = 1.38, 95% CI 1.18–1.62; p = 0.001). This finding suggests that invaded regions are not equivalent sources of invasion pressure: those experiencing more intense WNV transmission exert disproportionately greater influence on adjacent susceptible regions. These hazard ratios represent weighted average associations across the full study period; sensitivity analyses reported in the Supplementary Material confirm that both spatial-diffusion metrics remained strongly associated with invasion risk throughout, and that a modest departure from proportionality for distance and pressure does not alter the interpreted effects. Temperature remained the strongest climatic predictor after adjustment for spatial diffusion: each 1°C increase in annual mean temperature was associated with a 25% higher hazard of first emergence (HR = 1.25, 95% CI 1.19–1.31; p < 0.001). Relative humidity retained a modest negative association (HR = 0.96, 95% CI 0.93–0.99; p = 0.014), while precipitation was not independently associated with invasion risk in the multivariable model (HR = 0.99, 95% CI 0.85–1.14; p = 0.836). Urbanization category remained non- significant, with intermediate urban and rural regions showing 14% and 17% lower hazard than urban regions, respectively, though neither reached statistical significance. Taken together, these findings indicate that regional invasion risk is governed by both the geographic position of a susceptible region relative to existing invasion foci and the permissiveness of its local temperature, with spatial diffusion exerting the stronger and more consistent influence across all model specifications. The full multivariable model achieved a concordance (C-) statistic of 0.875, indicating strong discriminative performance. Introduction The emergence of a zoonotic vector-borne disease in a previously naïve area is rarely a purely stochastic event. It requires the concurrent alignment of multiple circumstances: a prospect for pathogen introduction, a competent host, suitable and abundant vectors, climatic suitability and a local environment permissive enough for establishment and onward transmission1. Global environmental change accelerates the emergence and spread of vector-borne diseases and their eco-climatic drivers have been previously described1–3. Yet, the process of pathogen diffusion, from existing foci to naïve areas, has not been disentangled and quantified. This knowledge asymmetry between the eco-climatic permissiveness of disease transmission and spatial pathogen diffusion remains one of the most salient gaps in contemporary infectious disease ecology. This discrepancy is particularly apparent for West Nile virus (WNV) in Europe. Sporadic European WNV outbreaks were documented from the late twentieth century onward, including Bucharest, Romania (1996–1997), the Czech Republic (1997), and Volgograd, Russia (1999)4,5. Since its resurgence across Europe in the early twenty-first century, WNV has spread from a few endemic foci in southeastern Europe to invade much of the continent, with outbreaks now reported at higher latitudes and in areas with no prior history of local circulation 6–8. This expansion has transformed WNV from a local episodic pathogen into a continent-wide zoonotic threat, yet the underlying mechanisms governing its geographic spread into previously disease-free areas have not been formally quantified. Eco-climatic drivers of WNV circulation, including temperature, humidity, vector ecology, and avian host availability, are increasingly Page 2/26 well understood, and future projections of WNV risk under climate change have been described6,9–11. What these frameworks cannot explain is the frontline of WNV invasion: why a particular region transitions from a disease-free to invaded in a particular year, while eco-climatically similar neighbouring regions remain naive. Answering this question requires moving beyond environmental and climatic suitability alone to consider spatial diffusion, the process by which WNV propagates outward from established foci across geographic space. For WNV, the virus circulates in an enzootic cycle between Culex mosquitoes and birds, and its geographic spread reflects the cumulative influence of interconnected local and migratory avian host populations and their movements, short-range mosquito dispersal, and recurring introduction events from surrounding WNV invaded areas.
